lessons.title: Africa: Overview, Introduction and Verse 1
lessons.description: Background, structure overview, and detailed analysis of the introduction and Verse 1 of Africa.
lessons.content_html:
Background to Toto — Africa

Africa is a song recorded by the American rock band Toto in 1981 for their fourth studio album, Toto IV. It is a soft-rock love song with features of African music. The song was written by band members David Paich (born 1954) and Jeff Porcaro (born 1954, died 1992).

Africa was released as the third single from the album on 30th September 1982 through Columbia Records. It reached number one in America for a single week on 5th February 1983. It also reached the top ten in the UK, Canada, Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand and Switzerland. In 2012, music magazine NME placed Africa at number 32 on its list of “50 Most Explosive Choruses”.

Key Fact

Instrumentation: rock band with drum kit and additional percussion, lead and bass guitars, synthesizers, male lead vocals and male backing vocals. The instrumental sonorities suggest African pitched percussion such as the kalimba and marimba. These sounds are made on a synthesiser, not on real instruments.

Overall Musical Elements

Before diving into the introduction and Verse 1, here are the key musical elements that apply across the whole song:

  • Tempo: Moderately fast.
  • Time signature: 2/2 (alla breve).
  • Dynamics: Most of the song is mezzo-forte, whilst the choruses are forte.
  • Form and structure: Verse–chorus form — Intro, Verse 1, Chorus 1, Link 1, Verse 2, Chorus 2, Link 2, Instrumental, Chorus 3, Chorus 4, Outro.

The key of this song is ambiguous. The verses and links can be interpreted in B major, E major, or A Lydian. The chorus, however, is clearly in A major. For the exam, use B major for the verses and A major for the choruses. Exam questions are written so that candidates can access marks whichever key they have been taught.

The Introduction (Bars 1–4)

The introduction is in the key of B major, so the intro chords A, G#m and C#m are labelled ♭VII, vi and ii. It is 4 bars long in the vocal score, but the recording also has an additional 8-bar percussion introduction before the scored intro begins. This percussion section uses layered rhythm parts and ostinatos, showing African musical influence.

The scored introduction contains only three chords: ♭VII (A), vi (G#m) and ii (C#m). It is built from two riffs, each lasting two bars:

Key Fact

Riff a (bars 1–2): A distinctive syncopated rhythm pattern, mostly repeating chord ♭VII (A) and concluding with chords vi (G#m) and ii (C#m). Riff b (bars 3–4, with an anacrusis): Uses an ostinato pattern of five notes based on the E major pentatonic scale over a sustained chord ii (C#m).

Both riffs have their origins in traditional African music. They use syncopation, a pentatonic scale, and irregular ostinato groupings that cut across the 2/2 time signature. The synthesised sounds imitate pitched percussion instruments found across the African continent, such as the kalimba and marimba.

Riff a is extremely important to the song’s structure. With the exception of the chorus, it appears in every other section. Riff b is developed later in the instrumental section. On the album version, the 4-bar intro section is played three times (giving 8 bars of percussion + 12 bars of Riff a and Riff b = 20 bars in total). Verse 1 enters at about 24 seconds. The single edit is shorter.

Use this mnemonic to remember the intro chords: Attack Graceful Camels Cats (and) Chimps — representing A (I/♭VII), G#m (vii/vi), C#m (iii/ii). The mnemonic works regardless of which key interpretation you use.

Verse 1 (Bars 5–39)

Verse 1 is 35 bars long and is in B major (with 5 sharps: F#, C#, G#, D# and A#, but all the A notes in this section are A naturals). The verse falls into four phrases:

Phrase 1

Bars 5–13 (9 bars)

“I hear the drums echoing tonight. She hears only whispers of some quiet conversation.”

Phrase 2

Bars 14–22 (9 bars)

“She’s coming in twelve thirty flight. Moonlit wings reflect the stars that guide me t’ward salvation.”

Phrase 3

Bars 23–31 (9 bars)

“I stopped an old man along the way, hoping to find some old forgotten words or ancient melodies.”

Phrase 4

Bars 32–39 (8 bars)

“He turned to me as if to say, ‘Hurry boy, it’s waiting there for you.’”

Why Are the Phrases 9 Bars Long?

A 9-bar phrase is unusual in popular music. The reason is that Riff a begins as the vocal line ends in bar 8 each time. This creates an overlap where the instrumental riff fills the gap before the next vocal phrase starts, adding an extra bar to each phrase.

The melody for the first three phrases is also unusual. Each phrase falls into two vocal lines of three and five bars, ending with a silent bar. The melody is fairly low in the voice, moves conjunctly (by step), uses a syncopated rhythm and is mostly syllabic (one note per syllable).

Verse 1 Harmony

The harmonic rhythm of the first three phrases is slow — chords change only once per bar, except the last bar where Riff a’s distinctive chord pattern appears. The 9-bar chord pattern for phrases 1–3 is:

Bar 5: I (B) → Bar 6: iii (D#m) → Bar 7: vi (G#m) → Bar 8: Ic (B/F#) → Bar 9: ♭VIIc (A/E) → Bar 10: IV9d (E/F#) → Bar 11: vi (G#m) → Bars 12–13: Riff a

For the 9-bar phrase: Bad Dogs Get Beaten And Evil Giraffes Attack Graceful Camels. Notice that the last two chords (A, G#m, C#m) are Riff a returning. Watch out for the slash chords (inversions): B/F#, A/E and E/F#. The first letter is the chord, the second letter is the bass note.

Phrase 4 — The Different Ending

The final phrase (bars 32–39) is only 8 bars long. It begins the same way as the first three phrases. However, in the fourth bar the melody begins an octave higher than previously stated. A backing vocalist harmonises the melody, moving in parallel motion at an interval of a 3rd below.

Harmonically, chord vi (G#m) is sustained for an extra bar. Riff a is then stated in bars 36–37, and chord ii (C#m) sustains until the end of the phrase. The chord pattern is:

Bar 32: I (B) → Bar 33: iii (D#m) → Bar 34: vi (G#m) → Bar 35: vi (G#m) → Bars 36–37: Riff a → Bar 38: ii (C#m) → Bar 39: ii (C#m)

Key Fact

Remember: All F, C and G chords in the song are sharp minor (#m) chords. The D chords are also sharp minor 7ths (D#m7) but only in the verse and instrumental sections. Watch out for slash chords — the first letter is the chord name, the second letter is the bass note.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the listening exam, you may be asked to identify specific features from the introduction or verse. Use precise bar numbers (e.g. “Riff a appears in bars 1–2”) and correct musical vocabulary like “syncopation”, “pentatonic scale” and “conjunct movement”. When describing the harmony, always give both the Roman numeral and the chord name (e.g. “vi — G#m”). If asked about African musical influences, mention the layered percussion ostinatos, syncopated rhythms, pentatonic scales and the synthesised kalimba and marimba timbres.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The introduction uses two riffs — Riff a (syncopated chords ♭VII, vi, ii) and Riff b (pentatonic ostinato over chord ii) — both influenced by traditional African music through syncopation, pentatonic scales and irregular groupings.
  • Verse 1 has four phrases: three 9-bar phrases (unusual length caused by Riff a overlapping with the vocal ending) and one 8-bar phrase with a different harmonic and melodic ending.
  • The verse melody is low, conjunct, syncopated and syllabic, with a slow harmonic rhythm (one chord per bar). Phrase 4 adds a backing vocal harmonising a 3rd below and shifts the melody up an octave.

glossary_terms.definition: A song recorded by the American rock band Toto in 1981, released as a single in 1982. It is a soft-rock love song with features of African music.
A style of rock music with a gentle, melodic sound, often featuring synthesizers and smooth vocal harmonies.
A short musical pattern that repeats continuously throughout a section or piece.
Placing rhythmic emphasis on beats or parts of beats that are not normally stressed, creating a feeling of rhythmic surprise.
A musical scale with five notes per octave, most commonly notes 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 of the major scale.
A short repeated phrase in popular music and jazz, typically used as an introduction or refrain in a song.
Moving by step from one note to the next adjacent note, rather than by leap.
A vocal style where each syllable of text is set to one note of music.
The rate at which the chords change in a piece of music.
Two or more parts moving in the same direction at the same time, maintaining a fixed interval between them.
A chord where a note other than the root is in the bass. Written as a slash chord, e.g. B/F# means a B chord with F# in the bass.

lessons.title: Africa: Chorus, Links, Verse 2 and Instrumental
lessons.description: Analysing the chorus harmony, link sections, verse 2 differences and the instrumental in Africa.
lessons.content_html:
Chorus 1 — Bars 40–57

After the long Verse 1 in B major, the music shifts to A major for the chorus. Chorus 1 is 18 bars long (4 + 4 + 4 + 6) and uses a repeating 4-bar chord sequence. It falls into four phrases:

Phrase 1 — Bars 40–43

Solo vocal

“It’s gonna take a lot to drag me away from you.” Sung by the lead vocalist alone.

Phrase 2 — Bars 44–47

Duet

“There’s nothing that a hundred men or more could ever do.” A second voice joins to create a duet.

Phrase 3 — Bars 48–51

Three parts

“I bless the rains down in Africa.” The texture thickens to three vocal parts.

Phrase 4 — Bars 52–57

Extended phrase (6 bars)

“Gonna take some time to do the things we never had.” The chord pattern changes and the melody ends with a melisma.

Chorus Melody

The melody for the first three phrases uses only two pitches: the tonic (A) and the leading note (G#). This is a huge contrast to the verse, where the melody sat low in the voice and moved conjunctly. In the chorus the melody is high in the voice, syncopated and syllabic — giving it a catchy, driving feel.

Key Fact

The chorus chord pattern for the first three phrases is vi–IV–I–V (F#m–D–A–E). This is a typical pop song chord progression. Remember the mnemonic: Fat Dogs Always Eat. The harmonic rhythm is one chord per bar, the same rate as the verse.

The Extended Fourth Phrase

The final phrase of each chorus (bars 52–57) is six bars long instead of four. It starts with the same vi–IV–I pattern, but the fourth bar introduces chord iii (C#m) instead of chord V. The full progression is:

vi (F#m) – IV (D) – I (A) – iii (C#m) – V (E) – vi (F#m) / Vb (E/G#)

The mnemonic for this is: Fat Dogs And Cats Eat Fried EGgs. The change to chord iii and the use of the slash chord E/G# at the end prepares the shift back to B major for the link section. The slash chord E/G# means an E chord with G# as the bass note — this is a first inversion (Vb).

The chorus begins with a solo voice, adds a second voice for phrase 2, then moves to three-part harmony for phrases 3 and 4. This gradual increase in the number of vocal parts thickens the texture and builds energy towards the climax of the chorus. The dynamics also shift to forte (f) in the chorus, compared with the mezzo-forte (mf) of the verses.

Link Sections — Bars 58–65

Link 1 and Link 2 are identical. They are both 8 bars long (4 + 4) and are in B major. Their job is to take us from the A major chorus back to B major for the next verse or instrumental section.

The chords are the same as the introduction: Riff a is played twice. The chord pattern for each 4-bar statement is ♮VII (A) – vi (G#m) – ii (C#m) – ii (C#m). Remember the mnemonic: All Good Cats Chase Cheese. While the introduction played Riff a three times, the links only play it once through (repeated), so they are shorter.

Key Fact

Riff a appears in every section of the song except the choruses. It uses syncopation and features the chords ♮VII, vi and ii in B major. In the links, Riff a is stated twice (8 bars total), compared with three times in the introduction.

Verse 2 — Bars 14–39

Verse 2 is in B major, just like Verse 1, and uses the same chord progressions. However, it is shorter: 26 bars (9 + 9 + 8) compared with 35 bars (9 + 9 + 9 + 8) in Verse 1. This is because the 9-bar phrase goes round twice instead of three times — one fewer repetition.

The three phrases are:

Phrase 1 — Bars 14–22 (9 bars)

“The wild dogs cry out in the night…”

“…as they grow restless, longing for some solitary company.”

Phrase 2 — Bars 23–31 (9 bars)

“I know that I must do what’s right…”

“…sure as Kilimanjaro rises like Olympus above the Serengeti.”

Phrase 3 — Bars 32–39 (8 bars)

“I seek to cure what’s deep inside…”

“…frightened of this thing that I’ve become.”

How Verse 2 Differs from Verse 1

Although Verse 2 reuses the same harmony as Verse 1, there are four key differences to know:

1. Fewer phrases: Verse 2 has three phrases (9 + 9 + 8 = 26 bars) instead of four (9 + 9 + 9 + 8 = 35 bars). This shortens the section by 9 bars.

2. Melodic change in bar 33: The singer leaps up to pitches D# and C# on the words “deep in,” which is different from the equivalent point in Verse 1.

3. Countermelody: A countermelody (or descant) played on a flute-like instrument is heard across the top of the texture. It changes pitch conjunctly and moves at the same speed as the harmonic rhythm.

4. More prominent backing vocals: In the two 9-bar phrases, backing vocals enter in the fifth bar, harmonising on “Ooo” before joining the lead singer with the last word of each phrase. At the start of the second 9-bar phrase, a backing vocalist harmonises initially a 4th higher than the melody, then continues a 3rd higher.

There is a clear pattern of shortening each time the verse material returns. Verse 1 has three 9-bar phrases plus one 8-bar phrase (35 bars). Verse 2 drops to two 9-bar phrases plus one 8-bar phrase (26 bars). The instrumental section drops further to one 9-bar phrase plus one 8-bar phrase (17 bars). Each time, one 9-bar repetition is removed. This creates a sense of momentum as the song progresses towards the final choruses.

Chorus 2 — Bars 40–57

Chorus 2 is identical to Chorus 1. It is 18 bars long, in A major, and uses the same vi–IV–I–V chord pattern for the first three phrases and the extended 6-bar pattern for the fourth phrase. After Chorus 2, Link 2 returns the music to B major, ready for the instrumental.

The Instrumental — Bars 66–82

The instrumental section is 17 bars long (9 + 8) and is in B major. It uses the same accompanying chords as the verse, but the vocal melody is almost entirely replaced by an instrumental melody based on Riff b. This is the shortest statement of the verse material, with only one 9-bar phrase before the final 8-bar phrase.

The instrumental melody can be broken down into four clear sub-sections:

Bars 66–69 (4 bars): A descending melody using a B major pentatonic scale. The notes fall into groups of three, ending with a triplet.

Bars 70–74 (5 bars): An ascending and descending melody using the E major scale. This passage has more rhythmic variety than the first half.

Bars 75–77 (3 bars): An ascending melody, also using the B major pentatonic scale with notes grouped in threes. It ends in a more “pop” style with the use of grace notes and syncopation.

Bars 78–82 (5 bars): The vocal part returns with the second half of the original 8-bar phrase: “Hurry boy, she’s waiting there for you.”

Key Fact

The instrumental melody develops Riff b from the introduction. It uses the B major pentatonic scale and the E major scale, with notes grouped in threes and featuring triplets, grace notes and syncopation. The vocal part only returns at bar 78 for the final five bars of the section.

There are a few important rules for the chords in Africa. All F, C and G chords in the song are sharp minor (e.g. F#m, C#m, G#m). The D chords are also sharp minor 7ths (D#m7) but only in the verse and instrumental sections — in the chorus, D is a major chord. Watch out for slash chords (inversions) such as E/G#: the first letter is the chord name and the second letter is the bass note.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the listening exam, you may be asked to identify specific features at given bar numbers. Make sure you know the exact bar ranges for each section (e.g. Chorus 1: bars 40–57, Link 1: bars 58–65, Instrumental: bars 66–82). Practise writing the chorus chord sequence from memory — vi–IV–I–V — and be ready to describe how Verse 2 differs from Verse 1. When describing melody, use precise terms like “conjunct,” “syllabic,” “melisma” and “pentatonic scale” rather than vague phrases like “it goes up and down.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The chorus is in A major with a vi–IV–I–V chord pattern (F#m–D–A–E). The melody uses only the tonic and leading note, is high in the voice, syncopated and syllabic, and the vocal texture builds from solo to three parts.
  • Verse 2 is 9 bars shorter than Verse 1 (26 bars vs. 35 bars) and adds a countermelody on a flute-like instrument, more prominent backing vocals, and a melodic change in bar 33 on the words “deep in.”
  • The instrumental (bars 66–82) is the shortest verse-based section at 17 bars. It develops Riff b into a full instrumental melody using the B major pentatonic and E major scales, with the vocal returning only for the final 5 bars.

lessons.title: Africa: Chorus 3, Outro and Exam Practice
lessons.description: Analyse Chorus 3 and the Outro, then practise exam technique for the Africa set work.
lessons.content_html:
Chorus 3 — Overview

Chorus 3 covers bars 40–92 of the score and is 22 bars long. Like all the choruses in Africa, it is in A major. This section repeats the music from Chorus 1 but with three notable changes that make it the climactic moment of the song.

The dynamics here are forte, continuing the pattern of the choruses being louder than the verses, which are mostly mezzo-forte. The texture remains homophonic, with a melody-and-accompaniment feel, but the added layers create a fuller, more intense sound.

Three Key Changes in Chorus 3

Chorus 3 is not identical to Chorus 1 or 2. There are three specific differences you must know for the exam:

Key Fact

The three changes in Chorus 3 are: (1) a new electric guitar riff in the last bar of each phrase, (2) Phrase 3 (“I bless the rains down in Africa”) is repeated five times instead of the usual number, making the section significantly longer, and (3) solo vocal improvisations are added at the end of the first, second and fourth repeats of Phrase 3.

A new electric guitar riff is heard on the recording in the last bar of each phrase (bars 43, 47, 51 etc.). This adds a fresh timbral layer not present in Choruses 1 or 2. It fills the gaps at the end of each four-bar phrase and helps drive the energy of the final chorus.

Phrase 3 — “I bless the rains down in Africa” — is heard five times during Chorus 3. This is significantly more than in the earlier choruses and makes this section the longest chorus in the song at 22 bars. The repetition builds intensity and drives the song towards its climax. This technique of repeating a hook line is common in popular music to make the most memorable part of the song feel bigger and more exciting.

During Phrase 3, a solo vocal improvisation is heard at the end of the first, second and fourth repeats. Each improvisation is different. The first two use the lyrics “I bless the rain,” while the final one uses “I’m gonna take some time.” These improvisations extend the pitch range of the vocal line beyond the less-than-two-octave range of the printed score, making the recording wider in range than the score suggests.

The Outro — Bars 93–96

The Outro begins at bar 93 and is 4 bars long in the score. It returns to B major, the key used for the majority of the song outside the choruses. The music repeats the material from the Introduction, using the chords of Riff a — the chords ♮VII, vi and ii (A, G#m and C#m in B major).

On the recording, this 4-bar phrase repeats continually. The key feature of the Outro is a gradual reduction in texture. Instruments drop out one by one until the music is reduced to only the rhythm track heard at the very beginning of the song, accompanied by the bass line of Riff a. The song ends with a fade out.

Key Fact

The Outro creates a circular structure: the song begins with layered percussion building up and ends with the texture stripping back down to that same percussion. This mirrors the Introduction and gives the song a sense of completion.

Putting the Whole Structure Together

Now that you have studied every section, it is important to see how the full structure fits together. Africa uses verse–chorus form:

Bars 1–4

Intro

B major. Riff a (syncopated chords) and Riff b (pentatonic ostinato). Played 3 times. Preceded on the recording by 8 bars of unpitched percussion.

Bars 5–39

Verse 1

B major. Four phrases (9+9+9+8 bars). Conjunct melody, syncopated, mostly syllabic. Riff a links phrases.

Bars 40–57

Chorus 1

A major. 18 bars (4+4+4+6). Forte dynamics. “Hurry boy” and “I bless the rains.”

Bars 58–65

Link 1

B major. 8 bars. Riff a chords twice.

Bars 14–39

Verse 2

B major. 26 bars (3 phrases not 4). Higher pitches on “deep in,” flute-like countermelody, more backing vocals.

Bars 40–57

Chorus 2

A major. 18 bars. Identical to Chorus 1.

Bars 58–65

Link 2

B major. 8 bars. Identical chords to Link 1 and Introduction (Riff a twice).

Bars 66–82

Instrumental

B major (with A naturals). 17 bars (9+8). Develops Riff b with ascending pentatonic melody. Grace notes and syncopation in ‘pop’ style ending.

Bars 40–92

Chorus 3

A major. 22 bars. New guitar riff, five repeats of “I bless the rains,” solo vocal improvisations.

Bars 93–96

Outro

B major. 4 bars repeated with gradual texture reduction and fade out. Uses Riff a chords.

Exam Technique: Answering Questions on Africa

In the listening exam, you may be asked questions about Africa using a printed score extract. Here are the key strategies:

Use bar numbers. Always refer to specific bar numbers when identifying features. For example, do not just say “in the chorus” — say “in bar 43.” You need to locate features precisely in the score.

Use correct musical vocabulary. Terms like syncopation, ostinato, pentatonic, conjunct, homophonic, diatonic, and riff should appear naturally in your answers. Avoid vague words like “catchy” or “nice.”

Cover multiple elements. The paper has one longer-response question, which expects you to discuss several musical elements — such as melody, rhythm, texture, harmony, dynamics, and instrumentation. Organise your answer by element to make sure you cover enough ground.

Key Fact

The paper tells you how many times each extract will be played. Use each playing to focus on different elements. First listening: melody and structure. Second: harmony and tonality. Third: rhythm and texture. Fourth: check and add detail.

Know what is on the score vs. what is on the recording. Some features — like the unpitched percussion intro, the electric guitar riff in Chorus 3, and the vocal improvisations — are heard on the recording but do not appear in the printed vocal score. The exam may ask about differences between the two.

Remember the key ambiguity. The standard analysis places the verses in B major, but the key could also be interpreted as E major or A lydian. The choruses are definitively in A major. Exam questions will accept any of these interpretations, so use whichever your teacher has taught.

Students often lose marks by: (1) forgetting that all F, C, and G chords in the song are sharp minor (#m) chords, (2) not mentioning slash chords (inversions) where the first letter is the chord and the second is the bass note (e.g. B/F#), (3) confusing what is in the score with what is only on the recording, and (4) writing about how the music makes them “feel” instead of describing what they can actually hear in musical terms.
lessons.exam_tip_html: If a question asks about features heard “on the recording,” make sure you include details not shown in the printed score — such as the vocal improvisations in Chorus 3 or the unpitched percussion at the very start. Avoid vague language: “the texture thins in the Outro as instruments drop out one by one” is far stronger than “it gets quieter at the end.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Chorus 3 (bars 40–92, A major, 22 bars) differs from earlier choruses with a new electric guitar riff, five repeats of “I bless the rains,” and solo vocal improvisations on the first, second and fourth repeats.
  • The Outro (bars 93–96, B major) uses Riff a chords, gradually reduces texture, and ends with a fade out — mirroring the Introduction.
  • In the exam, always use bar numbers, correct musical vocabulary, and cover multiple elements in extended responses. Know the difference between what is in the score and what is on the recording.

practice_questions.text: Africa by Toto has been described as a song that combines features of popular rock music with influences from African music. With reference to specific musical features heard across the whole song, discuss how both popular music and African music features are used in Africa. practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive, well-structured response covering both popular and African features with precise bar/section references and accurate terminology throughout.
Popular music features may include:
• Verse–chorus form typical of pop/rock songs
• Use of rock band instrumentation: drum kit, lead and bass electric guitars, synthesizers
• Male lead vocals with backing vocals
• Grace notes and syncopation used in a ‘pop’ style in the Instrumental
• Forte dynamics in choruses for impact
• Hook line repetition (‘I bless the rains’ x5 in Chorus 3)
• Fade out ending typical of pop production
• Diatonic harmony throughout
African music features may include:
• Syncopation throughout, especially in Riff a and vocal lines
• Use of the pentatonic scale (E major pentatonic in Riff b and Instrumental)
• Ostinato patterns in Riff b with irregular groupings that cut across the 2/2 time signature
• Layered rhythm parts in the unpitched percussion introduction
• Synthesised timbres suggesting African pitched percussion such as the kalimba and marimba
• Vocal improvisation in Chorus 3
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good range of points with mostly accurate vocabulary; may favour one side (pop or African) over the other.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant points but limited detail, few bar references, or inaccurate terminology.
Lower band (1-3): Basic observations with little structure or musical vocabulary.
